q: Methylbenzene (toluene) is heated with alkaline KMnO₄ and the mixture is then acidified. The organic product is:
x: Hot KMnO₄ oxidises the whole side chain of an alkylbenzene to –COOH, and acidifying the potassium benzoate frees benzoic acid. Stopping at the aldehyde or the alcohol is the tempting slip; those are only intermediate stages under these strong conditions.

q: 3.7 g of propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH (74 g mol⁻¹), is exactly neutralised by 0.50 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. What volume of NaOH is used?
x: Moles of acid = 3.7/74 = 0.050 mol; the acid is monobasic, so 0.050 mol NaOH is needed: 0.050/0.50 = 0.10 dm³ = 100 cm³. Treating the acid as dibasic gives 200 cm³; halving instead of dividing gives 50 cm³.

q: Which of these acids is the strongest?
x: The electron-withdrawing Cl stabilises the carboxylate ion, but its inductive effect weakens quickly with distance, so Cl on the carbon next to COOH (2-chlorobutanoic acid) has the greatest effect. Picking the 4-chloro acid comes from thinking the position of Cl does not matter.

q: Ethanoic acid reacts with phosphorus pentachloride, PCl₅. Besides ethanoyl chloride, the other products are:
x: CH₃COOH + PCl₅ → CH₃COCl + POCl₃ + HCl: the OH is replaced by Cl, the O goes to phosphorus and the H to HCl. Writing water as a by-product is the usual slip; water would hydrolyse the acyl chloride and is not formed.

q: Sodium propanoate is (i) heated with soda lime to give gas X, and separately (ii) its concentrated aqueous solution is electrolysed (Kolbe's method) to give hydrocarbon Y at the anode. X and Y are:
x: Soda lime removes CO₂: CH₃CH₂COONa + NaOH → CH₃CH₃ + Na₂CO₃, so X is ethane. In Kolbe electrolysis two CH₃CH₂COO⁻ ions each lose CO₂ and the two ethyl radicals join: Y is butane. Forgetting that the carboxyl carbon is lost gives propane and hexane.

q: A 0.10 mol dm⁻³ solution of a monobasic carboxylic acid has Ka = 1.6 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³. Its pH is about (log 2 = 0.30):
x: [H⁺] = √(Ka × c) = √(1.6 × 10⁻⁵) = 4 × 10⁻³, so pH = 3 − log 4 = 3 − 0.60 = 2.4. Treating it as a strong acid gives 1.0; forgetting the square root gives 4.8, and 3.8 is pKa.

q: Which carboxylic acid also gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent?
x: Methanoic acid, HCOOH, has an H on the carboxyl carbon, so it also behaves like an aldehyde and is oxidised to CO₂ and water, reducing Ag⁺ to silver. The other acids have no such H; choosing ethanoic acid confuses it with ethanal.

q: The ester formed when propan-1-ol is heated with ethanoic acid and a little concentrated H₂SO₄ is:
x: The ester is CH₃COOCH₂CH₂CH₃: the alcohol part is named first (propyl) and the acid part second (ethanoate). Swapping the two parts gives ethyl propanoate, a different ester.

q: Ethanoic anhydride, (CH₃CO)₂O, is warmed with ethanol. The products are:
x: (CH₃CO)₂O + C₂H₅OH → CH₃COOC₂H₅ + CH₃COOH: one acyl group goes to the alcohol and the other leaves as ethanoic acid. Writing water as the by-product mixes this up with esterification of the acid itself.

q: How many esters have the molecular formula C₄H₈O₂?
x: Methanoates: HCOOCH₂CH₂CH₃ and HCOOCH(CH₃)₂; ethanoate: CH₃COOCH₂CH₃; propanoate: CH₃CH₂COOCH₃; that is 4. Missing the branched methanoate gives 3, and counting the two acids C₃H₇COOH as well gives 6.

q: Ethanamide, CH₃CONH₂, is boiled with dilute hydrochloric acid. The products are:
x: Acid hydrolysis breaks the C–N bond: CH₃CONH₂ + H₂O + HCl → CH₃COOH + NH₄Cl, the ammonia being held as its salt. Sodium ethanoate and ammonia are the products of alkaline hydrolysis, the most tempting mix-up.

q: 6.0 g of ethanoic acid (60 g mol⁻¹) is heated with excess ethanol and a little concentrated H₂SO₄, and 5.28 g of ethyl ethanoate (88 g mol⁻¹) is obtained. The percentage yield is:
x: 0.10 mol of acid can give at most 0.10 mol = 8.8 g of ester; 5.28/8.8 × 100 = 60%. Dividing the ester mass by the acid mass (5.28/6.0) gives 88%, and 40% is the part not obtained.

q: Ethanoyl chloride reacts with methylamine, CH₃NH₂, to give compound P. P is then boiled with aqueous NaOH. The products of this second step are:
x: CH₃COCl + CH₃NH₂ → CH₃CONHCH₃ (N-methylethanamide) + HCl. Alkaline hydrolysis of this amide gives CH₃COONa and free CH₃NH₂. Ethanoic acid with methylammonium chloride would come from acid hydrolysis; splitting the molecule at the wrong carbon gives the methanoate/ethylamine pair.

q: Methyl methanoate, HCOOCH₃ (Mr 60), boils at about 32 °C while ethanoic acid (Mr 60) boils at 118 °C. The main reason is that methyl methanoate:
o: Has no O–H group, so its molecules cannot hydrogen-bond to each other
Has a smaller dipole moment because it has no C=O group
Has a lower molar mass than ethanoic acid
Forms hydrogen-bonded dimers that are easily broken
x: Both have the same Mr and both contain C=O, but only the acid has an O–H, so only the acid molecules are held by hydrogen bonds; the ester has only weaker dipole and dispersion forces. Saying the ester has no C=O is wrong, since every ester has one.

q: In the α-amino acids found in proteins, the amino group is attached to:
o: The carbon atom of the –COOH group
The carbon atom at the far end of the chain
The carbon atom next to the –COOH group
The oxygen atom of the –COOH group
x: α means the first carbon after the carboxyl carbon, so in H₂N–CHR–COOH the NH₂ and the side chain R share that carbon. Putting NH₂ on the carboxyl carbon itself would make an amide-like group, not an amino acid.

q: The IUPAC name of alanine, CH₃CH(NH₂)COOH, is:
x: The chain has three carbons including the COOH carbon, which is C-1, so NH₂ on the next carbon is at C-2: 2-aminopropanoic acid. Numbering from the CH₃ end gives 3-amino, and 2-aminoethanoic acid is glycine.

q: A mixture of glycine (pI 6.0), lysine (pI 9.7) and aspartic acid (pI 2.8) is placed at the centre of an electrophoresis strip in a buffer of pH 6.0, and a voltage is applied. What happens?
o: Lysine moves to the anode, aspartic acid to the cathode, glycine stays near the start
All three move to the cathode at different speeds
Glycine moves to the anode, lysine to the cathode, aspartic acid stays near the start
Aspartic acid moves to the anode, lysine to the cathode, glycine stays near the start
x: At a pH above its pI an amino acid is negative and moves to the anode (aspartic acid); below its pI it is positive and moves to the cathode (lysine); at its pI it has no net charge (glycine). Reversing the rule (pH above pI means positive) gives the swapped option.

q: Apart from glycine, the α-amino acids that make up natural proteins are almost all:
o: Racemic mixtures of D- and L-isomers
x: Every α-amino acid except glycine has a chiral α-carbon, and living things build proteins from the L-form only. Choosing a racemic mixture comes from thinking of laboratory synthesis, which does give both forms.

q: Which formula shows the dipeptide in which glycine provides the free –NH₂ end and alanine the free –COOH end?
x: The COOH of glycine condenses with the NH₂ of alanine to form –CO–NH–, leaving glycine's NH₂ and alanine's COOH free. The second formula is the other dipeptide (alanine at the NH₂ end); the ester link –COO– is not a peptide bond.

q: In the zwitterion of alanine, ⁺H₃NCH(CH₃)COO⁻, the group that donates a proton when a base such as NaOH is added is:
x: In the zwitterion the acidic proton is on nitrogen: ⁺H₃N– + OH⁻ → H₂N– + H₂O, giving the anion. The –COO⁻ group is the base, which accepts a proton from an acid; picking it mixes up the two roles.

q: 0.75 g of glycine (75 g mol⁻¹) reacts exactly with 0.10 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid, each glycine taking up one H⁺. What volume of acid is needed?
x: Moles of glycine = 0.75/75 = 0.010 mol, so 0.010 mol HCl is needed: 0.010/0.10 = 0.10 dm³ = 100 cm³ (the COO⁻ of the zwitterion becomes COOH). Leaving the answer as 0.10 dm³ read as 10 cm³ is a units slip; assuming two H⁺ per glycine gives 200 cm³.
